Reference: Freyaldenhoven, Hansen and Shapiro (2019)

Model Setting

The paper studies how to estimate the causal effect β\betaβ of a policy zitz_{it}zit​ on an outcome yity_{it}yit​ in a linear panel event-study design when strict exogeneity of the policy fails because a time-varying unobservable ηit\eta_{it}ηit​, the confound, is correlated with both the policy and the outcome. In the minimum wage literature yity_{it}yit​ is youth employment in state iii and year ttt, zitz_{it}zit​ indicates years after a minimum wage increase, and ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is labor demand: states tend to raise the minimum wage in good times (Card and Krueger 1995; Neumark and Wascher 2007). The common diagnostic is to look for pre-event trends (pre-trends), that is, apparent effects of the policy before it occurs. Of the 16 papers in the 2016 American Economic Review that use a linear panel data model, 11 are concerned with pre-trends, 9 plot them and only 2 test formally whether they are zero. The authors find this incomplete: if no pre-trend is detected, it may be present but missed for lack of power, and if one is detected, it is unclear what to do. What is needed is a notion of magnitude, namely how much of the apparent effect is due to the confound. The paper obtains it from a covariate xitx_{it}xit​ that is affected by the confound but not by the policy, an unaffected covariate (adult employment, which responds to labor demand but plausibly not to the minimum wage; Brown 1999). Instead of using xitx_{it}xit​ as a control, the paper uses its dynamics around the event to infer the dynamics of the confound. The main result is that β\betaβ can be estimated by two-stage least squares (2SLS) of the outcome on the policy and the covariate, with leads of the policy as excluded instruments, and that inference is valid whether or not pre-trends are present. In simulations the estimator beats controlling directly for xitx_{it}xit​ (unless xitx_{it}xit​ is a nearly perfect proxy), extrapolating a linear pre-trend, and pre-testing for pre-trends. Three applications illustrate cases where the adjustment barely matters (SNAP and food spending), changes the estimate by about 60 percent (SNAP and store-brand share), or leaves the parameter unidentified in practice (the minimum wage and teen employment).

To fix ideas, the outcome is observed for t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,Tt=1,…,T and the policy for t=1−L,…,T+Lt=1-L,\dots,T+Lt=1−L,…,T+L with L≥1L\geq1L≥1, for units i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,Ni=1,…,N, and:

yit=βzit+γηit+εit(1)y_{it}=\beta z_{it}+\gamma\eta_{it}+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{1}yit​=βzit​+γηit​+εit​(1)
E(εit∣ηit,{zit}t=1−LT+L)=0E(xit∣ηit,{zit}t=1−LT+L)=ληit(2)\begin{aligned} E\left(\varepsilon_{it}|\eta_{it},\{z_{it}\}_{t=1-L}^{T+L}\right)&=0\\ E\left(x_{it}|\eta_{it},\{z_{it}\}_{t=1-L}^{T+L}\right)&=\lambda\eta_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{2}E(εit​∣ηit​,{zit​}t=1−LT+L​)E(xit​∣ηit​,{zit​}t=1−LT+L​)​=0=ληit​​(2)

The first line is the causal model, the second assumes strict exogeneity of the policy with respect to εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​, and the third ties the covariate to the confound up to a nonzero scale λ\lambdaλ. If γ=0\gamma=0γ=0, identification is immediate. Otherwise, a regression of yity_{it}yit​ on {Δzi,t+l}l=−LL\{\Delta z_{i,t+l}\}_{l=-L}^{L}{Δzi,t+l​}l=−LL​ (with Δ\DeltaΔ the first difference) shows a pre-trend, and the same regression for xitx_{it}xit​ shows a similar pre-trend but a smaller jump at the event. The usual fixes each need a strong assumption: controlling for xitx_{it}xit​ works only if it is a perfect proxy (xit=ληitx_{it}=\lambda\eta_{it}xit​=ληit​), using yit−xity_{it}-x_{it}yit​−xit​ as outcome works only if γ=λ\gamma=\lambdaγ=λ, and extrapolating the pre-trend works only if the post-event path of the confound follows its pre-event trend. The proposal is geometric: rescale the event plot of the covariate so that it matches the event plot of the outcome in the two periods just before the event. Under the maintained assumptions the rescaled covariate traces the contribution of the confound, and the remaining gap at and after the event is the causal effect. The outcome event plot is a reduced form and the covariate event plot is a first stage, which leads to an instrumental variables estimator.

Model

The general model is a static linear panel:

yit=βzit+qit′θ+ηit′γ+αi+εitxit=qit′ψ+Ληit+νi+uit(3)\begin{aligned} y_{it}&=\beta z_{it}+q'_{it}\theta+\eta'_{it}\gamma+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{it}\\ x_{it}&=q'_{it}\psi+\Lambda\eta_{it}+\nu_i+u_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{3}yit​xit​​=βzit​+qit′​θ+ηit′​γ+αi​+εit​=qit′​ψ+Ληit​+νi​+uit​​(3)

where yity_{it}yit​ and zitz_{it}zit​ are observed scalars, qitq_{it}qit​ is an observed Q×1Q\times1Q×1 vector of exogenous controls (for example time indicators), xitx_{it}xit​ is an observed K×1K\times1K×1 vector of covariates, the latent factors ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ form an unobserved R×1R\times1R×1 vector, uitu_{it}uit​ is a K×1K\times1K×1 vector of measurement errors, εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​ is a scalar error, and αi\alpha_iαi​ and νi\nu_iνi​ are unrestricted unit fixed effects (a scalar and a K×1K\times1K×1 vector). The paper requires K≥RK\geq RK≥R and sets K=RK=RK=R for simplicity. The data are {yit,qit,xit}\{y_{it},q_{it},x_{it}\}{yit​,qit​,xit​} for i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,Ni=1,…,N and t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,Tt=1,…,T, and {zit}\{z_{it}\}{zit​} for t=1−m,…,T+ℓt=1-m,\dots,T+\ellt=1−m,…,T+ℓ with m≥0m\geq0m≥0 and ℓ≥R\ell\geq Rℓ≥R, so that enough leads of the policy are observed. The policy need not be binary. The controls are exogenous in the sense E[εit∣{qit}t=1T]=E[uit∣{qit}t=1T]=0E[\varepsilon_{it}|\{q_{it}\}_{t=1}^T]=E[u_{it}|\{q_{it}\}_{t=1}^T]=0E[εit​∣{qit​}t=1T​]=E[uit​∣{qit​}t=1T​]=0 and low-dimensional, Q≪NQ\ll NQ≪N. Two simplifications follow. First, θ=ψ=0\theta=\psi=0θ=ψ=0, which is without loss once all variables are read as residuals from a projection on the exogenous controls. Second, the fixed effects are removed by the within transformation k~it=kit−1T∑s=1Tkis\tilde{k}_{it}=k_{it}-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{s=1}^Tk_{is}k~it​=kit​−T1​∑s=1T​kis​, applied also to leads and lags (for example k~i,t−m=ki,t−m−1T∑s=1Tki,s−m\tilde{k}_{i,t-m}=k_{i,t-m}-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{s=1}^Tk_{i,s-m}k~i,t−m​=ki,t−m​−T1​∑s=1T​ki,s−m​); first differences would serve as well, with a matching reinterpretation of the assumptions. The model becomes:

y~it=βz~it+η~it′γ+ε~itx~it=Λη~it+u~it(4)\begin{aligned} \tilde{y}_{it}&=\beta\tilde{z}_{it}+\tilde{\eta}'_{it}\gamma+\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}\\ \tilde{x}_{it}&=\Lambda\tilde{\eta}_{it}+\tilde{u}_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{4}y~​it​x~it​​=βz~it​+η~​it′​γ+ε~it​=Λη~​it​+u~it​​(4)

The first equation is the outcome equation and the second is the measurement equation for the confound. The model is static: there are no anticipatory or dynamic effects (an extension below relaxes this), and the effect β\betaβ is homogeneous across units. The authors note that the recent literature on two-way fixed effects estimators under heterogeneous effects (Abraham and Sun 2018; Athey and Imbens 2018; de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille 2018; Goodman-Bacon 2018) suggests similar issues would arise here, but they do not develop heterogeneity or staggered-adoption corrections. Replacing ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ with xitx_{it}xit​ yields a factor or measurement error model; classical identification uses covariance restrictions across several noisy measurements, whereas this paper uses a single covariate and strict exogeneity of the policy with respect to its measurement error.

Identifying Assumptions

Assumption 1 (orthogonality). There is a set of nonnegative integers L={0,1,…,L}\mathcal{L}=\{0,1,\dots,L\}L={0,1,…,L} such that:

E[z~i,t+lε~it]=0,∀l∈LE[z~i,t+lu~it]=0,∀l∈L(5)\begin{aligned} E\left[\tilde{z}_{i,t+l}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}\right]&=0,\quad\forall l\in\mathcal{L}\\ E\left[\tilde{z}_{i,t+l}\tilde{u}_{it}\right]&=0,\quad\forall l\in\mathcal{L} \end{aligned} \tag{5}E[z~i,t+l​ε~it​]E[z~i,t+l​u~it​]​=0,∀l∈L=0,∀l∈L​(5)

Assumption 2 (rank). Define the instrument vector and the matrix:

wit=(z~it,z~i,t+1,…,z~i,t+L)′,H=E(wit[z~it,x~it′])(6)w_{it}=\left(\tilde{z}_{it},\tilde{z}_{i,t+1},\dots,\tilde{z}_{i,t+L}\right)',\qquad H=E\left(w_{it}\left[\tilde{z}_{it},\tilde{x}'_{it}\right]\right) \tag{6}wit​=(z~it​,z~i,t+1​,…,z~i,t+L​)′,H=E(wit​[z~it​,x~it′​])(6)

Then:

rank(Λ)=R,rank(H)=(R+1)(7)\mathrm{rank}\left(\Lambda\right)=R,\qquad\mathrm{rank}\left(H\right)=\left(R+1\right) \tag{7}rank(Λ)=R,rank(H)=(R+1)(7)

Assumptions 1 and 2 play the roles of the exclusion and relevance conditions of linear IV. Part (i) of Assumption 1 is implied by the strict exogeneity of the policy in the outcome equation that panel event studies usually assume: the policy and its leads may be correlated with the outcome only through the confound or through the causal effect. Part (ii) is implied by strict exogeneity of the policy in the covariate equation: the policy and its leads may be correlated with the covariate only through the confound. This rules out a causal effect of the policy on the covariate and any correlation between the policy and the measurement error uitu_{it}uit​. The two errors ε~it\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}ε~it​ and u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ need not be orthogonal, so the covariate may be correlated with the outcome through channels other than the confound, and the measurement errors may have arbitrary serial correlation (unlike Griliches and Hausman 1986, who instrument with lags of the mismeasured regressor). The first rank condition says the covariates carry information on every latent factor. The second is the usual relevance condition and is testable: it requires a nonzero correlation between xitx_{it}xit​ and the leads of zitz_{it}zit​, that is, a pre-trend in the covariate. Since γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 is allowed, the assumptions do not require a pre-trend in the outcome.

Two remarks connect the rank condition to economics. First, if rank(E(wit[z~it,η~it′]))=(R+1)\mathrm{rank}(E(w_{it}[\tilde{z}_{it},\tilde{\eta}'_{it}]))=(R+1)rank(E(wit​[z~it​,η~​it′​]))=(R+1), the second rank condition follows from Assumption 1, the first rank condition and the measurement equation, because E[witx~it′]=E[witη~it′]Λ′E[w_{it}\tilde{x}'_{it}]=E[w_{it}\tilde{\eta}'_{it}]\Lambda'E[wit​x~it′​]=E[wit​η~​it′​]Λ′ with Λ\LambdaΛ of full rank: a pre-trend in the confound implies a pre-trend in the covariate. Second, pre-trends in the confound are natural when the policy switches on once the confound crosses a threshold:

zit=1({∃t∗≤t:ηit∗>η∗})(8)z_{it}=\mathbf{1}\left(\left\{\exists t^{*}\leq t:\eta_{it^{*}}>\eta^{*}\right\}\right) \tag{8}zit​=1({∃t∗≤t:ηit∗​>η∗})(8)

If ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is autocorrelated, a crossing at t+1t+1t+1 signals that ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ was already close to the threshold at ttt, so the lead of the policy predicts the confound. Examples are a means-tested program that a household enters when the gap between its income and a poverty line passes a threshold (as in Ashenfelter 1978, where earnings dip before entry into job training), a firm that enters a market the first time the present value of cash flows, following a random walk, exceeds an entry trigger (McDonald and Siegel 1986; Dixit and Pindyck 1994), and a state that passes a law when the strength of its economy exceeds a threshold. The assumptions fail in a randomized controlled trial, where there is no pre-trend in the confound and the relevance condition fails, and with a poor covariate, where Λ=0\Lambda=0Λ=0 and the first rank condition fails; if Λ\LambdaΛ is nearly rank deficient, identification is weak. The rank condition becomes more demanding as RRR grows, so all simulations and applications use R=1R=1R=1, which approximates a model with several confounds that share similar dynamics around the event.

GMM Representation and 2SLS Estimator

Under the first rank condition define the vector:

Γ~=Λ(Λ′Λ)−1γ(9)\tilde{\Gamma}=\Lambda\left(\Lambda'\Lambda\right)^{-1}\gamma \tag{9}Γ~=Λ(Λ′Λ)−1γ(9)

which with K=RK=RK=R equals (Λ′)−1γ(\Lambda')^{-1}\gamma(Λ′)−1γ. Inverting the measurement equation gives η~it′γ=(x~it−u~it)′Γ~\tilde{\eta}'_{it}\gamma=(\tilde{x}_{it}-\tilde{u}_{it})'\tilde{\Gamma}η~​it′​γ=(x~it​−u~it​)′Γ~, and substituting into the outcome equation defines the composite error:

v~it≡ε~it−u~it′Γ~=y~it−βz~it−x~it′Γ~(10)\begin{aligned} \tilde{v}_{it}&\equiv\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}-\tilde{u}'_{it}\tilde{\Gamma}\\ &=\tilde{y}_{it}-\beta\tilde{z}_{it}-\tilde{x}'_{it}\tilde{\Gamma} \end{aligned} \tag{10}v~it​​≡ε~it​−u~it′​Γ~=y~​it​−βz~it​−x~it′​Γ~​(10)

The covariate stands in for the confound, but it is endogenous because its measurement error u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ enters the composite error. Both components of v~it\tilde{v}_{it}v~it​ are orthogonal to the policy and its leads by Assumption 1, which gives the moment conditions:

E[witv~it]=0(11)E\left[w_{it}\tilde{v}_{it}\right]=0 \tag{11}E[wit​v~it​]=0(11)

These conditions are linear in the parameters. Writing them as E[wity~it]=H(β,Γ~′)′E[w_{it}\tilde{y}_{it}]=H(\beta,\tilde{\Gamma}')'E[wit​y~​it​]=H(β,Γ~′)′, the second rank condition says HHH has full column rank, so the parameters are recovered uniquely:

(β,Γ~′)′=(H′H)−1H′E[wity~it](12)\left(\beta,\tilde{\Gamma}'\right)'=\left(H'H\right)^{-1}H'E\left[w_{it}\tilde{y}_{it}\right] \tag{12}(β,Γ~′)′=(H′H)−1H′E[wit​y~​it​](12)

This is the identification result: β\betaβ (and, incidentally, Γ~\tilde{\Gamma}Γ~) is identified. Estimation can proceed by GMM on the sample analogues of the moment conditions, with standard large-NNN, fixed-TTT asymptotics (Newey and McFadden 1994). A convenient special case is 2SLS of y~it\tilde{y}_{it}y~​it​ on z~it\tilde{z}_{it}z~it​ and x~it\tilde{x}_{it}x~it​, treating x~it\tilde{x}_{it}x~it​ as mismeasured regressors and the leads of z~it\tilde{z}_{it}z~it​ as excluded instruments. With R=K=L=1R=K=L=1R=K=L=1 the structural and first-stage equations are:

y~it=βz~it+Γ~x~it+v~itx~it=π0z~it+π1z~i,t+1+ς~itx(13)\begin{aligned} \tilde{y}_{it}&=\beta\tilde{z}_{it}+\tilde{\Gamma}\tilde{x}_{it}+\tilde{v}_{it}\\ \tilde{x}_{it}&=\pi_0\tilde{z}_{it}+\pi_1\tilde{z}_{i,t+1}+\tilde{\varsigma}^x_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{13}y~​it​x~it​​=βz~it​+Γ~x~it​+v~it​=π0​z~it​+π1​z~i,t+1​+ς~​itx​​(13)

where π0\pi_0π0​ and π1\pi_1π1​ are first-stage coefficients and ς~itx\tilde{\varsigma}^x_{it}ς~​itx​ is the first-stage error. Projecting the outcome on the policy and its lead gives the reduced form y~it=κ0z~it+κ1z~i,t+1+ς~ity\tilde{y}_{it}=\kappa_0\tilde{z}_{it}+\kappa_1\tilde{z}_{i,t+1}+\tilde{\varsigma}^y_{it}y~​it​=κ0​z~it​+κ1​z~i,t+1​+ς~​ity​ with κ0=β+Γ~π0\kappa_0=\beta+\tilde{\Gamma}\pi_0κ0​=β+Γ~π0​ and κ1=Γ~π1\kappa_1=\tilde{\Gamma}\pi_1κ1​=Γ~π1​, so the just-identified estimator is:

Γ~=κ1π1,β=κ0−Γ~π0(14)\tilde{\Gamma}=\frac{\kappa_1}{\pi_1},\qquad\beta=\kappa_0-\tilde{\Gamma}\pi_0 \tag{14}Γ~=π1​κ1​​,β=κ0​−Γ~π0​(14)

This is the geometry of the event plots. Because the policy affects the covariate only through the confound, the ratio of the pre-trend in the outcome to the pre-trend in the covariate measures how strongly the confound moves the outcome; the covariate's jump at the event, scaled by this ratio, is the part of the outcome's jump due to the confound, and the rest is β\betaβ. The standard event-study estimator is the case Γ~=0\tilde{\Gamma}=0Γ~=0, and controlling for xitx_{it}xit​ by OLS is the case that ignores u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ and is biased by attenuation. The estimator from Gentzkow, Shapiro and Sinkinson (2011, appendix), which combines a dynamic first stage with a static second stage, is close in spirit but not justified by this setup.

Practical remarks. Any functions of the leads z~i,t+l\tilde{z}_{i,t+l}z~i,t+l​, l∈Ll\in\mathcal{L}l∈L, are valid instruments, but with moderate TTT the closest leads are the most informative, so the default is the RRR closest leads, which makes the model just identified. If y~it\tilde{y}_{it}y~​it​ and z~it\tilde{z}_{it}z~it​ are observed in one sample and x~it\tilde{x}_{it}x~it​ and z~it\tilde{z}_{it}z~it​ in another, two-sample IV (Angrist and Krueger 1992; Inoue and Solon 2010) applies. Plausible violations of the exclusion restrictions can be handled with methods for locally misspecified moments (Conley, Hansen and Rossi 2012; Andrews, Gentzkow and Shapiro 2017); because part (i) of Assumption 1 is the usual strict exogeneity, part (ii) is expected to be the more controversial one. In an event plot estimated with the lead as an instrument, one more coefficient must be normalized (the paper sets δ−2=0\delta_{-2}=0δ−2​=0 in addition to δ−1=0\delta_{-1}=0δ−1​=0), and precision depends on the normalization chosen. With weak first stages, inference should use weak-identification robust methods (Stock, Wright and Yogo 2002; Andrews and Mikusheva 2016).

Monte Carlo Design

The data-generating processes have an autoregressive confound, threshold-crossing policy, a single covariate and an outcome with a linear time trend:

ηit=ρηi,t−1+ζit,ζit∼N(0,σζ2)xit=ληit+uit,uit∼N(0,σu2)(15)\begin{aligned} \eta_{it}&=\rho\eta_{i,t-1}+\zeta_{it},\qquad\zeta_{it}\sim N\left(0,\sigma^2_{\zeta}\right)\\ x_{it}&=\lambda\eta_{it}+u_{it},\qquad u_{it}\sim N\left(0,\sigma^2_u\right) \end{aligned} \tag{15}ηit​xit​​=ρηi,t−1​+ζit​,ζit​∼N(0,σζ2​)=ληit​+uit​,uit​∼N(0,σu2​)​(15)
yit=βzit+0.25ηit+0.2t+αi+εit(16)y_{it}=\beta z_{it}+0.25\eta_{it}+0.2t+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{16}yit​=βzit​+0.25ηit​+0.2t+αi​+εit​(16)

where the policy follows the threshold rule above, β=1\beta=1β=1, αi∼N(0,1)\alpha_i\sim N(0,1)αi​∼N(0,1) and εit∼N(0,1)\varepsilon_{it}\sim N(0,1)εit​∼N(0,1), and all shocks are i.i.d. and mutually independent. The benchmark has λ=ρ=1\lambda=\rho=1λ=ρ=1, σζ2=1\sigma^2_{\zeta}=1σζ2​=1 and σu2=4\sigma^2_u=4σu2​=4, starts from ηi1=0\eta_{i1}=0ηi1​=0, simulates 20 periods and estimates on t=6,…,15t=6,\dots,15t=6,…,15. The broader designs vary ρ∈[0,0.9]\rho\in[0,0.9]ρ∈[0,0.9] and choose σζ2\sigma^2_{\zeta}σζ2​ and σu2\sigma^2_uσu2​ so that var(η~it)=1\mathrm{var}(\tilde{\eta}_{it})=1var(η~​it​)=1 and var(x~it)=2\mathrm{var}(\tilde{x}_{it})=2var(x~it​)=2, with a 20-period burn-in from a standard normal draw, N=1,000N=1{,}000N=1,000 units, T=10T=10T=10 and about 200 units with an event (all units, treated or not, are used). A higher ρ\rhoρ strengthens the instruments (and also the bias from ignoring the confound); λ\lambdaλ is varied to move the population R2R^2R2 of the infeasible regression of xitx_{it}xit​ on ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ between 0 (no signal, no identification) and 1 (perfect proxy).

Dynamic estimates come from the event-study regression with binned endpoints:

yit=δ−6+(1−zi,t+5)+δ5+zi,t−5+∑k=−45δ−kΔzi,t+k+ωt+αi+ηit+εit(17)y_{it}=\delta_{-6+}\left(1-z_{i,t+5}\right)+\delta_{5+}z_{i,t-5}+\sum_{k=-4}^{5}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+\omega_t+\alpha_i+\eta_{it}+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{17}yit​=δ−6+​(1−zi,t+5​)+δ5+​zi,t−5​+k=−4∑5​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+ωt​+αi​+ηit​+εit​(17)

where Ω\OmegaΩ is the slope of the trend, identified from event times −3-3−3 to −1-1−1, and each δk\delta_kδk​ is the deviation from the trend. Static estimates come from:

yit=βzit+ωt+αi+ηitγ+εit(19)y_{it}=\beta z_{it}+\omega_t+\alpha_i+\eta_{it}\gamma+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{19}yit​=βzit​+ωt​+αi​+ηit​γ+εit​(19)

where the trend extrapolation estimator uses the average post-event deviation β^=15∑k=−40δ^−k\hat{\beta}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{k=-4}^{0}\hat{\delta}_{-k}β^​=51​∑k=−40​δ^−k​. Event plots report both pointwise 95 percent intervals and uniform 95 percent sup-t bands (Olea and Plagborg-Moller 2019), which contain the whole true path with probability 0.95 and are more informative about which pre-trends the data allow.

Monte Carlo Results

  • Benchmark: in a single draw, failing to control shows strong pre-trends and post-event estimates around 1.3 to 1.6 against a true value of 1; controlling for xitx_{it}xit​ only partly removes the bias; the 2SLS plot is centered on the truth but noisier than the infeasible one, because the pre-trend in xitx_{it}xit​ is modest; the linear trend understates the confound right after the event and overstates it later; and the pre-test detects no pre-trend, so its plot equals the uncontrolled one. Across 5,000 simulations only 2SLS is centered at the true value, and the pre-test fails to detect the pre-trend in 2,930 of them.

  • Bias and dispersion over the design space (2,000 replications per point): failing to control is severely biased everywhere; controlling for xitx_{it}xit​ is badly biased unless the R2R^2R2 of xitx_{it}xit​ on ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is close to 1; 2SLS has small median bias and median absolute deviation except where identification is weak (low R2R^2R2 or low ρ\rhoρ); trend extrapolation is biased throughout; pre-testing barely improves on no control, because even at ρ=0.9\rho=0.9ρ=0.9 the pre-test rejects in fewer than 30 percent of simulations although a pre-trend is always present in population.

  • Coverage: nominal 95 percent intervals have coverage near 95 percent for 2SLS except in weakly identified regions, and poor coverage for the other feasible estimators. Pre-testing mixes coverage of 1 (when it gives up) with coverage near 0 (when it proceeds with a biased estimate).

Applications: SNAP and Newspapers

SNAP and household spending (Hastings and Shapiro 2018). Units are Rhode Island households and periods are quarters; zitz_{it}zit​ indicates quarters after entry into SNAP, the confound is income (eligibility requires low income), and xitx_{it}xit​ is average monthly household income (in-state earnings and unemployment insurance) from administrative data. Outcomes, from a retailer panel, are at-home food expenditure and the store-brand share of food spending. Since yity_{it}yit​ and xitx_{it}xit​ are in different samples, two-sample IV is used. The covariate event study is:

xit=δ−5+(1−zi,t+4)+δ5+zi,t−5+∑k=−44δ−kΔzi,t+k+ϕt+νi+uit(20)x_{it}=\delta_{-5+}\left(1-z_{i,t+4}\right)+\delta_{5+}z_{i,t-5}+\sum_{k=-4}^{4}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+\phi_t+\nu_i+u_{it} \tag{20}xit​=δ−5+​(1−zi,t+4​)+δ5+​zi,t−5​+k=−4∑4​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+ϕt​+νi​+uit​(20)

and the outcome event study is:

yit=δ−5+(1−zi,t+4)+δ5+zi,t−5+∑k=−44δ−kΔzi,t+k+γηit+αi+ωt+εit(21)y_{it}=\delta_{-5+}\left(1-z_{i,t+4}\right)+\delta_{5+}z_{i,t-5}+\sum_{k=-4}^{4}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+\gamma\eta_{it}+\alpha_i+\omega_t+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{21}yit​=δ−5+​(1−zi,t+4​)+δ5+​zi,t−5​+k=−4∑4​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+γηit​+αi​+ωt​+εit​(21)

where ϕt\phi_tϕt​ and ωt\omega_tωt​ are time effects. Income declines clearly before adoption and recovers afterwards. Food expenditure shows no meaningful pre-trend, so the adjustment changes little; the store-brand share shows a pre-trend that is small in absolute terms but large relative to the jump at adoption, and 2SLS removes it. Here the exclusion restriction requires that SNAP does not directly change cash income, which would fail if entry, or its anticipation, reduced labor supply. In the static version, the effect on monthly food expenditure is 85.97 dollars (1.23) with no control and 84.35 dollars (1.11) with 2SLS; the effect on the store-brand share is −0.0044-0.0044−0.0044 (0.0004) with no control and −0.0070-0.0070−0.0070 (0.0004) with 2SLS, almost 60 percent larger in magnitude. The first-stage coefficient on the lead is −151.81-151.81−151.81 (2.55). Linear trend extrapolation instead implies a small initial effect that grows over time, and the pre-test procedure gives up for the store-brand share because it rejects δ−2=0\delta_{-2}=0δ−2​=0.

Newspapers and turnout (Gentzkow, Shapiro and Sinkinson 2011). Units are counties and periods are presidential election years; zitz_{it}zit​ is the number of English-language daily newspapers, the confound is market profitability, and xitx_{it}xit​ is the log of the voting-eligible population. In first differences, with state-year effects ϕst\phi_{st}ϕst​ and ωst\omega_{st}ωst​:

Δxit=∑k=−55δ−kΔzi,t+k+Δϕst+ΔuitΔyit=∑k=−55δ−kΔzi,t+k+Δωst+γΔηit+Δεit(22)\begin{aligned} \Delta x_{it}&=\sum_{k=-5}^{5}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+\Delta\phi_{st}+\Delta u_{it}\\ \Delta y_{it}&=\sum_{k=-5}^{5}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+\Delta\omega_{st}+\gamma\Delta\eta_{it}+\Delta\varepsilon_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{22}Δxit​Δyit​​=k=−5∑5​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+Δϕst​+Δuit​=k=−5∑5​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+Δωst​+γΔηit​+Δεit​​(22)

Population growth rises before entry and flattens afterwards. The exclusion restriction requires that newspaper entry and exit do not affect population or its relation to profitability. The effect of one more newspaper on turnout is 0.0026 (0.0009) with no control, 0.0037 (0.0010) controlling for xitx_{it}xit​, and 0.0034 (0.0013) with 2SLS, with first-stage coefficient 0.0128 (0.0017). Cluster-bootstrap ppp-values (100 replications) for equality with the estimate that controls for xitx_{it}xit​ are 0.000 for no control and 0.714 for 2SLS.

Application: Minimum Wage and Teen Employment

Units are states and periods are quarters. The outcome yity_{it}yit​ is the log teen (ages 16 to 19) employment-to-population ratio, the policy zitz_{it}zit​ is the log of the prevailing (higher of federal and state) minimum wage from David Neumark's dataset, the control qitq_{it}qit​ is the teen share of the population, and the confound ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is labor demand. The covariate xitx_{it}xit​ is the log prime-age (25 to 55) employment-to-population ratio. The exclusion restriction requires that the minimum wage does not affect prime-age employment or its relationship to labor demand, plausible because the minimum wage matters little for prime-age workers relative to other sources of variation (Brown 1999); directly controlling for xitx_{it}xit​, as is common, ignores that it measures youth labor demand with error. Data come from the CPS Outgoing Rotation Groups for 1985 to 2014, regressions are weighted by teen population and standard errors are clustered by state. The covariate event study, where qitq_{it}qit​ excludes time indicators, is:

xit=δ−4+(1−zi,t+3)+δ3+zi,t−3+∑k=−23δ−kΔzi,t+k+qit′ψ+ϕt+νi+uit(23)x_{it}=\delta_{-4+}\left(1-z_{i,t+3}\right)+\delta_{3+}z_{i,t-3}+\sum_{k=-2}^{3}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+q'_{it}\psi+\phi_t+\nu_i+u_{it} \tag{23}xit​=δ−4+​(1−zi,t+3​)+δ3+​zi,t−3​+k=−2∑3​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+qit′​ψ+ϕt​+νi​+uit​(23)

and the outcome event study is:

yit=δ−4+(1−zi,t+3)+δ3+zi,t−3+∑k=−23δ−kΔzi,t+k+γηit+qit′θ+ωt+αi+εit(24)y_{it}=\delta_{-4+}\left(1-z_{i,t+3}\right)+\delta_{3+}z_{i,t-3}+\sum_{k=-2}^{3}\delta_{-k}\Delta z_{i,t+k}+\gamma\eta_{it}+q'_{it}\theta+\omega_t+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{it} \tag{24}yit​=δ−4+​(1−zi,t+3​)+δ3+​zi,t−3​+k=−2∑3​δ−k​Δzi,t+k​+γηit​+qit′​θ+ωt​+αi​+εit​(24)

Point estimates show prime-age employment rising before minimum wage increases (roughly −0.05-0.05−0.05 to −0.04-0.04−0.04 in log points two to three quarters before, relative to the quarter before), but the uniform bands cannot reject no pre-trend. The static model in first differences is:

Δyit=βΔzit+Δqit′θ+Δωt+γΔηit+Δεit(25)\Delta y_{it}=\beta\Delta z_{it}+\Delta q'_{it}\theta+\Delta\omega_t+\gamma\Delta\eta_{it}+\Delta\varepsilon_{it} \tag{25}Δyit​=βΔzit​+Δqit′​θ+Δωt​+γΔηit​+Δεit​(25)

The elasticity of teen employment with respect to the minimum wage is −0.0114-0.0114−0.0114 (0.0743) with no control and −0.0094-0.0094−0.0094 (0.0708) controlling for prime-age employment, both insignificant. The proposed 2SLS estimator, which instruments the change in log prime-age employment with the first lead of the change in the log minimum wage, gives 0.0003 (0.0668). The first-stage coefficient on the lead is 0.0314 (0.0136), a weak first stage: the confidence set for the coefficient on xitx_{it}xit​ from inverting the Anderson-Rubin test is the whole real line, so by projection the confidence interval for β\betaβ is [−∞,∞][-\infty,\infty][−∞,∞], and the same holds for the dynamic coefficients of the 2SLS event plot. This is the limitation of the method: identification needs a strong pre-trend in the covariate, and without one the econometrician cannot learn β\betaβ; the authors argue this is the right conclusion when one worries about a confound and does not trust xitx_{it}xit​ to be a perfect proxy.

In 2SLS, y~it\tilde{y}_{it}y~​it​ is regressed on {z~i,t−m}m=−GM\{\tilde{z}_{i,t-m}\}_{m=-G}^{M}{z~i,t−m​}m=−GM​ and x~it\tilde{x}_{it}x~it​, and only the leads beyond GGG serve as excluded instruments: anticipation uses up the nearest leads, so the instruments must come from further ahead.

Overidentification. With more than RRR leads, BIC is a natural way to choose among the ordered candidate leads (Rao et al. 2001), efficient GMM applies, and the overidentifying restrictions can be tested. Such a test is the formal counterpart of checking for remaining pre-trends in the 2SLS event plot, but selecting a model on the basis of the test brings the usual pre-test biases (Leeb and Potscher 2005; Guggenberger 2010). With more covariates than confounds (K>RK>RK>R), standard moment selection and combination methods weight the covariates efficiently, with the same caveats. Alternatively, measurement-error methods can identify the model without using leads as instruments: with R=1R=1R=1, K=2K=2K=2 and errors u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ uncorrelated across covariates and with ε~it\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}ε~it​, a rank condition analogous to Assumption 2 suffices. With many covariates carrying independent information on the confounds, high-dimensional factor methods could be adapted (Stock and Watson 2002; Bai 2003).

References

  • Freyaldenhoven, Simon, Christian Hansen, and Jesse M Shapiro. 2019. “Pre-Event Trends in the Panel Event-Study Design.” American Economic Review, 109(9): 3307–3338.

This is the motivating causal model of the introduction, written for the simplest case of one confound and one covariate. The outcome yity_{it}yit​ of unit iii in period ttt depends on the policy zitz_{it}zit​ through the causal effect β\betaβ, the parameter of interest, and on the unobserved confound ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ through γ\gammaγ; εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​ is everything else. In the minimum wage example yity_{it}yit​ is youth employment, zitz_{it}zit​ marks years after a minimum wage increase, and ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is labor demand, so γ>0\gamma>0γ>0.

The problem is that ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is correlated with the policy path: states raise the minimum wage in good times. A regression of yity_{it}yit​ on zitz_{it}zit​ then converges to

β+γ cov⁡(zit,ηit)var⁡(zit)\beta+\gamma\,\frac{\operatorname{cov}(z_{it},\eta_{it})}{\operatorname{var}(z_{it})}β+γvar(zit​)cov(zit​,ηit​)​

which is biased whenever γ≠0\gamma\neq0γ=0. Nothing is assumed about how ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ evolves or how it triggers the policy; the equation only says that, holding the confound fixed, the policy shifts the outcome by β\betaβ, the same for all units and periods (homogeneous and static effects). If γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 the confound is irrelevant and an ordinary event study identifies β\betaβ. Equation (3) generalizes this to vector confounds, controls and fixed effects, and equation (26) adds anticipatory and dynamic effects.

These two conditional moment restrictions complete the introductory model of equation (1). They condition on the confound in period ttt and on the entire observed policy path, from 1−L1-L1−L to T+LT+LT+L, so they are strict exogeneity assumptions: past, current and future policy carry no information about εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​ or about the covariate once ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is known. (The index ttt is reused as the running index of the path; read the set as all periods of the policy history of unit iii.)

The first line rules out feedback from the error of the outcome to the policy, beyond what runs through ηit\eta_{it}ηit​. The second line is the substantive new assumption: the covariate xitx_{it}xit​ is, in expectation, a scaled copy of the confound, with a nonzero scale λ\lambdaλ, and the policy does not move it except through ηit\eta_{it}ηit​. Writing xit=ληit+uitx_{it}=\lambda\eta_{it}+u_{it}xit​=ληit​+uit​, it says

E(uit∣ηit,{zis}s=1−LT+L)=0E\left(u_{it}|\eta_{it},\{z_{is}\}_{s=1-L}^{T+L}\right)=0E(uit​∣ηit​,{zis​}s=1−LT+L​)=0

so the measurement error is unrelated to the policy path, including its leads. This is what later makes leads of the policy valid instruments for the covariate (equation (5)). Note what is not assumed: xitx_{it}xit​ need not equal ληit\lambda\eta_{it}ληit​ (that would be a perfect proxy), γ\gammaγ need not equal λ\lambdaλ, and uitu_{it}uit​ may be correlated with εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​. Adult employment in the minimum wage application is an example: it tracks labor demand with noise and is plausibly unaffected by the minimum wage.

This is the general static linear panel model. The first line is the outcome equation: yity_{it}yit​ depends on the scalar policy zitz_{it}zit​ with effect β\betaβ, on QQQ observed exogenous controls qitq_{it}qit​ (for example time dummies) with coefficients θ\thetaθ, on the R×1R\times1R×1 vector of latent factors ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ with loadings γ\gammaγ, on a unit fixed effect αi\alpha_iαi​ and on an error εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​. The second line is the measurement equation: the K×1K\times1K×1 vector of covariates xitx_{it}xit​ loads on the same factors through the K×RK\times RK×R matrix Λ\LambdaΛ, has its own control coefficients ψ\psiψ and fixed effects νi\nu_iνi​, and is observed with a K×1K\times1K×1 measurement error uitu_{it}uit​.

The specification is a linear factor model in which the factors also confound the policy. Its key restrictions are: the policy does not appear in the covariate equation (an unaffected covariate), the effect β\betaβ is homogeneous and contemporaneous, and the fixed effects are unrestricted, so time-invariant differences in levels between units are harmless. With R=K=1R=K=1R=K=1, γ\gammaγ a scalar and Λ=λ\Lambda=\lambdaΛ=λ, and without controls or fixed effects, it reduces to equations (1) and (2). The data requirement that zitz_{it}zit​ is observed up to T+ℓT+\ellT+ℓ with ℓ≥R\ell\geq Rℓ≥R ensures that at least RRR leads of the policy exist in every estimation period, which is the number of excluded instruments needed later (equation (7)). Setting θ=ψ=0\theta=\psi=0θ=ψ=0 and removing fixed effects gives equation (4).

Start from equation (3) with the simplification θ=ψ=0\theta=\psi=0θ=ψ=0 (all variables read as residuals from a projection on qitq_{it}qit​):

yit=βzit+ηit′γ+αi+εit,xit=Ληit+νi+uity_{it}=\beta z_{it}+\eta'_{it}\gamma+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{it},\qquad x_{it}=\Lambda\eta_{it}+\nu_i+u_{it}yit​=βzit​+ηit′​γ+αi​+εit​,xit​=Ληit​+νi​+uit​

Subtract the averaged equation from the period-ttt equation. The terms αi\alpha_iαi​ and νi\nu_iνi​ cancel, and each remaining variable becomes its deviation from the unit mean, k~it=kit−1T∑s=1Tkis\tilde{k}_{it}=k_{it}-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{s=1}^Tk_{is}k~it​=kit​−T1​∑s=1T​kis​:

y~it=βz~it+η~it′γ+ε~itx~it=Λη~it+u~it\begin{aligned} \tilde{y}_{it}&=\beta\tilde{z}_{it}+\tilde{\eta}'_{it}\gamma+\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}\\ \tilde{x}_{it}&=\Lambda\tilde{\eta}_{it}+\tilde{u}_{it} \end{aligned}y~​it​x~it​​=βz~it​+η~​it′​γ+ε~it​=Λη~​it​+u~it​​

This is equation (4). Linearity is what makes the transformation commute with the model. The price is that each ε~it\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}ε~it​ and u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ contains the errors of all periods 1,…,T1,\dots,T1,…,T, so orthogonality conditions stated for transformed variables (equation (5)) are implied by strict exogeneity of the whole policy path rather than by contemporaneous exogeneity. Taking first differences instead would also remove αi\alpha_iαi​ and νi\nu_iνi​, with errors Δεit\Delta\varepsilon_{it}Δεit​ and Δuit\Delta u_{it}Δuit​.

This is Assumption 1, the exclusion restriction of the proposed IV strategy. L={0,1,…,L}\mathcal{L}=\{0,1,\dots,L\}L={0,1,…,L} indexes the current policy and its first LLL leads, all within-transformed. Line one says that the policy and its leads are uncorrelated with the outcome error ε~it\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}ε~it​; line two says that they are uncorrelated with the measurement error u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ of every covariate.

Line one is the standard condition behind panel event studies: it follows from strict exogeneity of the policy in the outcome equation, so the policy and its leads can be related to y~it\tilde{y}_{it}y~​it​ only through the causal effect or the confound. Line two follows from strict exogeneity in the measurement equation: the policy path may predict x~it\tilde{x}_{it}x~it​ only because it predicts η~it\tilde{\eta}_{it}η~​it​. This rules out any causal effect of the policy (or of its anticipation) on the covariate, and any correlation between the policy path and the measurement error. In the SNAP application it fails if anticipated program entry reduces labor supply and hence measured income.

What is not required matters as much. ε~it\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}ε~it​ and u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​ may be correlated with each other, so the covariate may enter the outcome through channels other than the confound, and both errors may be serially correlated. The leads may be correlated with the confound; indeed they must be, for relevance (equation (7)). The moment conditions in equation (11) are built directly from these two lines.

These are the objects of Assumption 2. The instrument vector witw_{it}wit​ stacks the within-transformed policy in period ttt and its LLL leads, so it is (L+1)×1(L+1)\times1(L+1)×1. Leads are used rather than lags because the policy at t+lt+lt+l cannot cause the covariate at ttt once anticipation is ruled out, whereas lags could be contaminated by any delayed effect.

This is Assumption 2, the relevance condition. The first part says that the K×RK\times RK×R loading matrix has full column rank, so the covariates carry independent information on every latent factor; with K=RK=RK=R it means Λ\LambdaΛ is invertible. It fails with a poor covariate (Λ=0\Lambda=0Λ=0), and identification is weak when Λ\LambdaΛ is nearly rank deficient. It is what allows the definition of Γ~\tilde{\Gamma}Γ~ in equation (9).

The second part requires the (L+1)×(R+1)(L+1)\times(R+1)(L+1)×(R+1) matrix HHH of equation (6) to have full column rank R+1R+1R+1. This needs L≥RL\geq RL≥R (at least as many leads as confounds) and a nonzero relation between the leads and the covariate beyond what the current policy explains, that is, a pre-trend in xitx_{it}xit​. It fails in a randomized experiment, where the leads are independent of the confound. Because γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 is allowed, no pre-trend in the outcome is required.

This is the threshold-crossing assignment rule (Remark 4 of the paper) that motivates why the relevance condition in equation (7) is natural. The policy indicator zitz_{it}zit​ equals one from the first period t∗t^{*}t∗ at which the scalar confound ηit∗\eta_{it^{*}}ηit∗​ exceeds the threshold η∗\eta^{*}η∗, and stays at one afterwards: the policy is an absorbing state triggered by the confound. The same rule generates the policy in the Monte Carlo designs of equations (15) and (16), with η∗\eta^{*}η∗ tuned so that about 200 of 1,000 units experience an event.

Why does this create a pre-trend in the confound? Suppose ηit=ρηi,t−1+ζit\eta_{it}=\rho\eta_{i,t-1}+\zeta_{it}ηit​=ρηi,t−1​+ζit​ with ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0. Since ηi,t+1=ρηit+ζi,t+1\eta_{i,t+1}=\rho\eta_{it}+\zeta_{i,t+1}ηi,t+1​=ρηit​+ζi,t+1​, crossing next period is more likely when ηit\eta_{it}ηit​ is already high, so

Economic examples are means-tested programs entered after income falls, firm entry when the present value of cash flows hits an entry trigger, and laws passed when the economy is strong.

This extends the outcome equation of equation (4) to anticipatory and dynamic effects. The outcome now depends on the policy from GGG periods ahead to MMM periods back: βm\beta_mβm​ is the effect of the policy mmm periods after it is in place, so m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,Mm=1,…,M are dynamic (lagged) effects, m=0m=0m=0 is the contemporaneous effect and m=−G,…,−1m=-G,\dots,-1m=−G,…,−1 are anticipation effects of a policy that will be in place ∣m∣|m|∣m∣ periods later. The confound term, the error and the measurement equation are unchanged, and GGG and MMM are taken as known.

The extension shows how the identification strategy adapts. Anticipation means the leads z~i,t+1,…,z~i,t+G\tilde{z}_{i,t+1},\dots,\tilde{z}_{i,t+G}z~i,t+1​,…,z~i,t+G​ now affect the outcome directly, so they become included regressors and can no longer be excluded instruments; only leads beyond GGG can serve, which is why the orthogonality conditions in equation (27) run to G+LG+LG+L. With G=M=0G=M=0G=M=0 the sum collapses to β0z~it\beta_0\tilde{z}_{it}β0​z~it​ and the static model is recovered. A cost of anticipation is weaker instruments: leads further from the event are generally less correlated with the current confound. Because Γ~\tilde{\Gamma}Γ~ is defined as before from equation (9), the composite error in equation (29) has the same form as in equation (10).

This is Assumption 1 for the dynamic model of equation (26). The set L\mathcal{L}L now runs from −M-M−M (lags of the policy) to G+LG+LG+L (leads): it includes the MMM lags and GGG near leads that enter the outcome equation as regressors, the current policy, and LLL further leads G+1,…,G+LG+1,\dots,G+LG+1,…,G+L that serve as excluded instruments. For every such lll, the policy at t+lt+lt+l must be uncorrelated with the outcome error ε~it\tilde{\varepsilon}_{it}ε~it​ and with each covariate's measurement error u~it\tilde{u}_{it}u~it​.

As in equation (5), the first condition is implied by strict exogeneity of the policy path in the outcome equation, and the second by strict exogeneity in the covariate equation (no effect of the policy, its anticipation or its lags on the covariate, and no correlation with the measurement error). Unlike in the static case, L\mathcal{L}L contains negative integers: the lags z~i,t−m\tilde{z}_{i,t-m}z~i,t−m​ are regressors, so they must also be exogenous. LLL is a positive integer; it must be at least RRR for the rank condition in equation (28). These conditions say nothing about the correlation between the policy and the confound, which is left unrestricted.

These are the objects of Assumption 2 in the dynamic model. The instrument vector witw_{it}wit​ stacks the within-transformed policy from t−Mt-Mt−M to t+G+Lt+G+Lt+G+L, so it is (M+G+L+1)×1(M+G+L+1)\times1(M+G+L+1)×1. The bracket lists the regressors of the dynamic estimating equation: the M+G+1M+G+1M+G+1 policy terms z~i,t−M,…,z~i,t+G\tilde{z}_{i,t-M},\dots,\tilde{z}_{i,t+G}z~i,t−M​,…,z~i,t+G​ (which instrument themselves) and the KKK covariates. HHH is therefore (M+G+L+1)×(M+G+1+K)(M+G+L+1)\times(M+G+1+K)(M+G+L+1)×(M+G+1+K).

The rank conditions are rank(Λ)=R\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda)=Rrank(Λ)=R, as before, and rank(H)=R+M+G+1\mathrm{rank}(H)=R+M+G+1rank(H)=R+M+G+1, which with K=RK=RK=R is full column rank. Counting rows and columns,

M+G+L+1≥M+G+1+R  ⟺  L≥RM+G+L+1\geq M+G+1+R\iff L\geq RM+G+L+1≥M+G+1+R⟺L≥R
